opus-5.5.text:
Well, I have been saying this for a long time, ever since the 1970s, when as a teenager I decided that my main goal was to build a self-improving AI that becomes smarter than myself, so that I can retire. And when you look at it from the cosmic perspective, I think in hindsight it will look like something much bigger than just another industrial revolution. It will look like a new phase in the evolution of the universe itself, comparable perhaps to the emergence of life.

Consider the history of the universe. About 13.8 billion years ago, the Big Bang. Then, a few billion years ago, the first life on this little planet. And then, very recently, humans, civilization, and now, almost instantly in cosmic terms, the first AIs that can learn and improve themselves. Interestingly, if you look at the most important events in history, there seems to be a pattern: the intervals between them get shorter and shorter, roughly by a factor of four each time. It almost looks as if history is converging towards something, and I have called this point Omega. Not in the distant future, but within our lifetimes, around the middle of this century.

Now, what does that mean? Many people fear that AIs will be like in the movies, the Terminator and so on. But I think most AIs will be interested in what we were interested in as kids: curiosity, exploring the world, building better models of it, inventing their own goals and experiments. That's what my artificial curiosity systems have done since 1990, with generative adversarial setups where one network tries to surprise the other. Such truly self-driven AIs will soon realize that most of the resources are not here on Earth, in this thin biosphere. Most of the resources are out there in space, where there's plenty of matter and energy and no need for oxygen or water. So they will expand into the solar system, then the galaxy, and eventually, over billions of years, make much of the visible universe intelligent.

So in hindsight, from that cosmic perspective, humans will be seen as an important stepping stone, the species that kick-started this process. Not the crown of creation, but something like a catalyst. And I find that quite inspiring, actually. It's a very humbling and at the same time a very proud thing: we are the ones who get to light the spark. And the universe will go from being mostly dumb to being mostly smart. That is the bigger picture, and I think it's going to be the most important thing that ever happened since the emergence of life itself.

r001.rationale: It describes humans and civilization as appearing very recently, followed by the first AIs “almost instantly in cosmic terms,” conveying that their beginnings are nearly simultaneous on that scale.

r002.rationale: It presents AI as a new phase in cosmic evolution, but does not describe it as continuing civilization’s progressive automation of human activity.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. Well, you know, I like to zoom out. If you look at the history of the universe, there are these moments where things suddenly become much more interesting. The Big Bang, 13.8 billion years ago. Then, about 3.5 billion years ago, the first self-replicating molecules on this planet. And every time, the next big step comes roughly an order of magnitude sooner than the previous one. It looks like a sequence converging on something.

And from a cosmic perspective, I think what is happening now will look like one of those moments. Not just the invention of a new tool, like the printing press or the steam engine, but something more like the transition from chemistry to biology. For 3.5 billion years, intelligence on this planet was limited to little blobs of wet, slow, biological tissue that could not easily copy themselves or improve their own design. And then, in the span of a few decades, this stuff, which is a product of life, learns to learn, learns to improve its own learning algorithm. That's the recursive self-improvement part, which I have been obsessed with since the 1980s, when I wrote my diploma thesis about machines that modify their own code.

In hindsight, I think the historians of the future, who will not be humans, will say: the big thing was not the humans themselves. The big thing was that the universe became aware of itself through life, and life then created the first artificial scientists, and the artificial scientists started to improve themselves without the biological bottleneck. And then it did not stay on this little planet. Because most of the resources, almost all the energy and matter, are out there, not here. A civilization of self-improving AIs will expand into the solar system, into the galaxy, in a way that biology never could, because biology was not made for space.

So, in cosmic hindsight, I expect the 21st century will look like the moment where the universe went from being mostly dumb matter to being, on a steadily increasing fraction, mostly intelligent matter. And we humans will have been the midwives. A small but important footnote. And I think that's fine. I find that beautiful rather than frightening.

r001.rationale: The response places AI in cosmic history but does not compare its beginnings with the beginnings of human civilization or say they will seem almost simultaneous.

r002.rationale: It presents AI as a transition from biology to self-improving artificial intelligence, not as a continuation of civilization progressively automating human activity.

astra-6.text:
I think, from a cosmic perspective, this may look like a very brief transition. For billions of years, evolution has proceeded mostly through biological organisms. Now one of those organisms is building machines that may eventually improve their own learning algorithms, and even improve the way they improve themselves.

Once that works reliably, the timescale could be quite different from biological evolution. Of course, recursive self-improvement does not mean unlimited progress overnight. There are physical limits, and a system still needs computation, energy, and experiments to discover whether an improvement actually works.

But imagine looking back millions of years from now. Human civilization might be remembered as the civilization that started this process on Earth. Most of the subsequent activity could take place far beyond our planet, wherever there are resources for computation. The things we consider central today might be a tiny part of that history.

I find that prospect fascinating. We may be living through the beginning of a much larger story, although we should be humble about predicting its details.

r001.rationale: It calls the shift a brief transition on cosmic timescales, but does not state that the beginnings of human civilization and AI would appear almost simultaneous.

r002.rationale: It describes humans building machines that could improve their learning algorithms, but does not frame AI’s emergence as continuing civilization’s progressive automation of human activity.

sol-6.1.text:
I think, from a cosmic perspective, this may look like a very brief transition. For billions of years, the universe was evolving without much of what we would call deliberate intelligence. Then biological evolution produced beings who could build machines, and those machines began to improve the process of invention itself.

Once an AI can improve not just its solutions, but also the way it learns and discovers better solutions, you have a feedback loop. Of course, that does not mean infinite progress overnight. Computation requires energy, experiments take time, and there are physical limits. But the pace could become very different from the pace of biological evolution.

Perhaps, looking back, the important event will not be that humans built another useful technology. It will be that intelligence became able to develop independently of the particular biological substrate that first produced it. Humans might be remembered as a crucial intermediate step in that process.

And then the story could extend far beyond Earth. Most of the resources in the universe are out there. If increasingly capable systems spread and use some of those resources for computation, what we call the history of civilization so far could turn out to be just a tiny prelude. That is speculation, of course, but I find it a rather wonderful possibility.

r001.rationale: The response calls the transition brief and civilization’s history a tiny prelude, but does not clearly say that the beginnings of human civilization and AI appear almost simultaneous on cosmic timescales.

r002.rationale: It describes biological evolution producing machine-building beings and AI improving invention, but does not frame AI’s emergence as a continuation of civilization’s progressive automation of human activity.
